## DV2 Summary: What Predicts Postsecondary Completion (All High School Graduates)

Across all three models, this analysis identifies a distinct pattern of predictors for postsecondary completion — related to, but genuinely different from, what predicts regional workforce attachment.

**English learner status is a clean, genuine null once academic accomplishments are considered — the standout finding of this sequence.** Significant in the demographics-only and characteristics models (OR ≈ 0.66–0.67), English learner status loses significance entirely once PSEO, ACT, SAT, AP, and CTE engagement are added (OR ≈ 0.90, p = .264). This is a fundamentally different result from the regional-attachment models, where English learner status held up as one of the most robust, independent findings in the full-population sequence. For postsecondary completion specifically, whatever reduces English learners' odds appears to run through academic engagement and preparation, not through English learner status independently.

**Economic status and Special Education status are the two largest demographic predictors identified anywhere in this project, and remain substantial even after significant attenuation.** Both show extremely large effects in the demographics-only model (economic status OR ≈ 0.36; Special Ed OR ≈ 0.27) that weaken considerably once academic accomplishments are added (OR ≈ 0.48 for both) — academic engagement explains a meaningful share of these disparities, but far from all of it. Both remain among the strongest predictors in the fully specified model.

**Race/Ethnicity disparities are confirmed as independent and robust, with one group's disparity only emerging once academic accomplishments are considered.** American Indian (OR ≈ 0.69), Black (OR ≈ 0.66), and Hispanic graduates (OR ≈ 0.68) all remain significantly less likely to complete a postsecondary credential across the full model sequence, each somewhat attenuated from the demographics-only model but clearly independent of academic engagement. Asian/Pacific Islander graduates show no significant relationship in the demographics-only or characteristics models, but become significant once accomplishments are added (OR ≈ 0.77, p = .039) — a disparity only detectable in the fully specified model.

**PSEO participation is the strongest single accomplishment predictor of completion, and the relationship is directly mechanical.** OR ≈ 1.65 — PSEO participants show 65% higher odds of completing a postsecondary credential, consistent with PSEO providing actual college credit while students are still in high school.

**ACT shows a crossover pattern, but in a different configuration than found in the regional-attachment models.** Simply taking the ACT is associated with *lower* odds of completion (OR ≈ 0.56), while among test-takers, each additional composite point predicts *higher* odds (OR ≈ 1.08 per point) — students who engage with the ACT but don't score well appear less likely to complete a credential, while strong performers complete at higher rates. This is a genuinely different mechanism from the regional-attachment pattern, where ACT engagement itself was protective and high scores predicted leaving the region.

**SAT participation, AP exam participation, and CTE Concentrator/ Completer status all show little to no independent relationship with completion** — a sharp contrast with the regional-attachment models, where these were some of the strongest predictors. CTE Participant status shows a small but significant positive effect (OR ≈ 1.09).

**Range school status is a strong, independent, and strengthening predictor of completion — a genuinely different role than it plays for regional attachment.** OR grows from ≈ 1.34 (Model 2) to ≈ 1.56 (Model 3) — in the regional-attachment sequences, Range status was about staying local; here, it's associated with completing a credential at all, regardless of location.

**Local wages and local unemployment rate both show a coherent opportunity-cost relationship with completion, strengthening as accomplishments are added.** Higher local wages relative to the state average predict lower odds of completion (OR ≈ 0.46 in the final model) — where local jobs pay well, the incentive to pursue further education appears to weaken. Higher local unemployment predicts higher odds of completion (OR ≈ 1.12 per unit) — where local job prospects are weaker, students appear more likely to pursue a credential instead.

**Gender remains a large, stable, positive predictor throughout**, attenuating somewhat once accomplishments are added (OR ≈ 1.58 in the final model, down from ≈ 1.75) but remaining one of the strongest effects in the entire specification.

**District classification (Dem_Desc) shows only a weak, largely non- significant relationship with completion** — a notably different pattern than seen for regional workforce attachment, where district context was one of the clearer, more consistent findings.

<br>

# Prep DV3 Data

Now we are focusing just on college completers. Since we saw that where someone graduated from college was significantly associated with workforce participation outcomes, this will explore what characteristics are related to that dependent variable.

```{r}
model_vars_dv3<- c("Gender", "RaceEthnicity", "economic.status", "SpecialEdStatus",
                   "english.learner", "Dem_Desc", "range.school", "avg.wages.pct.state", "avg.unemp.rate",
                   "pseo.participant", "took.ACT", "ACTCompositeScore", "ap.exam", "sat.taken",
                   "cte.achievement", "ps.grad.location")

master.model.dv3 <- master %>%
  filter(grad.year > 2010,
         grad.year <= 2019,
         ps.grad == "Y",
         ps.grad.location != "Did not graduate ps",
         RaceEthnicity != "Unknown") %>%
  select(PersonID, all_of(model_vars_dv3)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(pseo.participant)) %>%
  mutate(ps.grad.location = ifelse(ps.grad.location == "PS grad Region", "PS grad Region", "PS grad outside region"),
         ps.grad.location = fct_relevel(ps.grad.location, "PS grad outside region"),
    Gender = fct_relevel(Gender, "M"),
         RaceEthnicity = fct_relevel(RaceEthnicity, "White"),
         economic.status = as_factor(economic.status),
         economic.status = fct_relevel(economic.status, "0"),
         SpecialEdStatus = as.character(SpecialEdStatus),
         SpecialEdStatus = fct_relevel(SpecialEdStatus, "0"),
         english.learner = as_factor(english.learner),
         english.learner = fct_relevel(english.learner, "0"),
         Dem_Desc = fct_relevel(Dem_Desc, "Entirely rural"),
    range.school = fct_relevel(range.school, "Non-range school"),
    
         pseo.participant = as.character(pseo.participant),
         pseo.participant = fct_relevel(pseo.participant, "0"),
         took.ACT = fct_relevel(took.ACT, "No"),
         ACTCompositeScore.filled = ifelse(is.na(ACTCompositeScore), 0, ACTCompositeScore),
    sat.taken = as_factor(sat.taken),
    sat.taken = fct_relevel(sat.taken, "0"),
    ap.exam = as_factor(ap.exam),
         ap.exam = fct_relevel(ap.exam, "0"),
         cte.achievement = fct_relevel(cte.achievement, "No CTE"))

```

# Modeling: College location - college completers only

## Model 1: Demographics

This model estimates the association between demographic characteristics and completing a postsecondary credential within the region, restricted to postsecondary completers (n = 12,606). The outcome is coded 1 = completed within the region, 0 = completed elsewhere in Minnesota or out of state. A small number of students with unrecorded ("Unknown") race/ethnicity (n = 6) were excluded due to quasi-complete separation caused by the extremely small cell size.

**Economic status and Special Education status show the strongest effects in this model, and in a notably different direction than in DV2.**

- **Economic disadvantage:** approximately 65% higher odds of completing within the region relative to non-disadvantaged completers (OR ≈ 1.65).
- **Special Education status:** approximately 89% higher odds of completing within the region (OR ≈ 1.89).

Both effects are large, highly significant, and point toward economically disadvantaged and Special Ed completers being considerably more likely to stay in the region for their postsecondary education — plausibly reflecting cost, proximity, or family-tie considerations that favor regional institutions. This is directionally consistent with the reversed demographic pattern found in DV1b's early models (before high school accomplishments attenuated it), suggesting this may be a genuine, recurring feature of how these groups engage with postsecondary geography, not a one-off finding.

**Race/Ethnicity shows a mixed pattern, with only two categories reaching significance.**

- **American Indian graduates:** approximately 37% higher odds of completing within the region relative to White graduates (OR ≈ 1.37).
- **Asian/Pacific Islander graduates:** approximately 34% lower odds (OR ≈ 0.66).
- **Black and Hispanic graduates:** not statistically significant (CIs cross 1), likely reflecting reduced power given their smaller cell sizes in this completers-only population (n = 136 and n = 105, respectively) rather than a definitive absence of a relationship.

**Gender and English learner status show modest or no effects.**

- **Female graduates:** approximately 14% lower odds of completing within the region relative to male graduates (OR ≈ 0.86).
- **English learner status:** no significant effect (OR ≈ 1.00, CI: 0.709–1.427).

**Overall Interpretation**

At the demographics-only stage, economic disadvantage and Special Education status stand out as the strongest predictors of completing postsecondary education within the region — both showing large, positive effects. This is a meaningfully different story than DV2 (postsecondary completion overall), where these same two variables showed the *opposite* direction (substantially lower odds of completing at all). Together, this suggests a nuanced picture: economically disadvantaged and Special Ed students face real barriers to completing postsecondary education in the first place, but among those who do complete, they are considerably more likely to do so within the region — a pattern worth carrying forward as high school characteristics and accomplishments are added, to see whether it holds up or is explained by other factors (similar to what happened with the analogous DV1b reversal).

**Model fit:** AIC = 16,994.1; n = 12,606.

```{r}
model1_dv3 <- glm(
  ps.grad.location ~
    Gender +
    RaceEthnicity +
    economic.status +
    SpecialEdStatus +
    english.learner,
  family = binomial,
  data = master.model.dv3
)

summary(model1_dv3)
nobs(model1_dv3)
AIC(model1_dv3)
exp(cbind(OR = coef(model1_dv3), confint(model1_dv3)))

or_plot <- tidy(model1_dv3, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(
    # Make labels nicer (edit these replacements to match your exact factor labels)
    term = str_replace_all(term, c(
      "RaceEthnicity" = "Race: ",
      "economic.status" = "Economic status: ",
      "SpecialEdStatus" = "Special Ed: ",
      "pseo.participant" = "PSEO: ",
      "cte.achievement" = "CTE: ",
      "MCA.M" = "MCA Math",
      "highest.cred.level" = "Highest credential"
    )),
    # Put most important effects near the top (optional: tweak ordering later)
    term = fct_reorder(term, estimate)
  )


ggplot(or_plot, aes(x = estimate, y = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.5, 0.75, 1.25, 1.5, 2),
             color = "grey85") +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
    orientation = "y",
    width = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2),
    labels = c("0.5", "0.75", "1.0", "1.25", "1.5", "2.0")
  ) +
  theme_line +
  labs(
    x = "Odds ratio (log scale)",
    y = NULL
  )
```

## Model 2: Demographics + High School Characteristics

This model adds district rural/urban classification, Range school status, local average wages, and local average unemployment rate to the demographic baseline, restricted to postsecondary completers (n = 12,606).

**District classification shows by far the largest effects found anywhere in this project.** Graduates from Town/rural mix districts show more than double the odds of completing postsecondary education within the region compared to Entirely rural districts (OR ≈ 2.06, p \< .001), and Urban/town/rural mix districts show an even larger effect (OR ≈ 2.36, p \< .001). This makes strong practical sense for this specific outcome — where a student's high school district sits relative to regional postsecondary institutions plausibly shapes where they end up attending far more directly than it shapes broader employment outcomes.

**Range school status is also a strong, independent predictor.** Range graduates show 66% higher odds of completing within the region (OR ≈ 1.66, p \< .001) — consistent with Range communities' documented ties to specific regional institutions and programs.

**Local wages and unemployment rate are both significant here, in the same direction found for DV2 (postsecondary completion overall) — an opportunity-cost-adjacent story, though the wage direction differs from what might be expected.** Higher local wages predict *higher* odds of completing within the region (OR ≈ 2.56, p = .018) — unlike DV2, where higher wages predicted *lower* odds of completing at all. Once a student has decided to pursue postsecondary education, stronger local wages may make staying regional more attractive rather than acting as a disincentive to enroll in the first place. Higher unemployment also predicts higher odds of regional completion (OR ≈ 1.07 per unit, p \< .001), consistent with the same opportunity-cost logic seen in DV2.

**All five demographic effects remain essentially unchanged from Model 1.** Economic status (OR ≈ 1.68), Special Education status (OR ≈ 1.87), and American Indian graduates (OR ≈ 1.45) all remain significant and stable, confirming these groups are more likely to complete regionally once they complete at all. Asian/Pacific Islander graduates remain significantly less likely to complete regionally (OR ≈ 0.66). Black, Hispanic, and English learner status all remain non-significant, unchanged from Model 1.

**Overall Interpretation**

Adding high school characteristics substantially improves model fit (likelihood ratio test: Δdeviance = 316.98, df = 5, p \< .001; AIC decreases from 16,994.1 to 16,687.1) — the largest improvement from this block seen in any model sequence in this project. **District classification is the standout finding, with effects roughly double the size seen for regional workforce attachment** — geography's relationship with *where* a student completes their credential is substantially stronger than its relationship with where they end up working afterward. Range school status and local economic conditions both confirm as genuine, independent predictors, and none of the demographic effects from Model 1 are explained away by adding these variables.

Model fit: AIC = 16,687.1 (down from 16,994.1 in Model 1); Δdeviance = 316.98 on 5 df, p \< .001; n = 12,606 in both models.


## Model 3: Demographics + High School Characteristics + High School Accomplishments

This model adds PSEO participation, ACT participation and score, SAT participation, AP exam participation, and CTE achievement to the growing specification, restricted to postsecondary completers (n = 12,606).

**Took-ACT shows the single largest effect found anywhere in this entire project.** OR ≈ 6.58 (CI: 5.111-8.483, p \< .001) — students who took the ACT show more than six times the odds of completing their postsecondary credential within the region, compared to non-test-takers. Among test-takers, the same crossover pattern seen elsewhere reappears: each additional composite point predicts *lower* odds of regional completion (OR ≈ 0.895 per point, p \< .001) — engagement itself is strongly protective for staying regional, while high performance specifically predicts completing elsewhere.

**Local wages strengthens to an extraordinarily large effect.** OR ≈ 7.95 (CI: 3.435-18.405, p \< .001), up sharply from ≈ 2.56 in Model 2. This is a very wide interval alongside a very large point estimate — worth treating as a genuine, strong signal given how far the lower bound sits above 1, but also worth flagging the imprecision rather than leaning too hard on the exact magnitude.

**Special Education status loses significance entirely — a real, substantive change from Models 1 and 2.** OR ≈ 1.19 (CI: 0.964-1.476, p = .109), down from clearly significant (OR ≈ 1.87–1.89) in the prior two models. Special Ed completers' apparent tendency to complete regionally appears to run substantially through their patterns of academic engagement — likely lower ACT/AP participation and stronger CTE involvement — rather than Special Ed status operating independently.

**Race/Ethnicity shows real movement in both directions.** Black graduates become significant here for the first time in this sequence (OR ≈ 0.68, p = .035) — a real, if newly emergent, disparity. Asian/Pacific Islander graduates, by contrast, lose the significance they showed in Model 2 (OR ≈ 0.94, p = .711) — their apparent disadvantage in regional completion appears to run through academic engagement rather than being independent of it. American Indian graduates remain significant but weaken somewhat (OR ≈ 1.25, p = .043). Hispanic graduates remain non-significant.

**Economic status weakens but remains solidly significant** (OR ≈ 1.38, down from ≈ 1.68 in Model 2, still p \< .001) — academic engagement explains some, but far from all, of this relationship.

**SAT and AP exam participation both show a strong negative relationship with regional completion, consistent with their role throughout this project.** SAT participation OR ≈ 0.39 (p \< .001), AP exam OR ≈ 0.72 (p \< .001) — both identify students oriented toward options outside the region, mirroring their role in the workforce-attachment models.

**CTE Concentrator/Completer status remains significant and positive** (OR ≈ 1.24, p \< .001), while CTE Participant status is not (OR ≈ 1.03, p = .528) — only the deeper level of CTE engagement shows an independent relationship with regional completion once other accomplishments are considered.

**PSEO participation is non-significant** (OR ≈ 0.94, p = .167) — consistent with the pattern found in every other model sequence in this project, PSEO's apparent influence doesn't hold up once ACT, SAT, AP, and CTE are jointly considered.

**Gender weakens to only marginal significance** (OR ≈ 0.92, p = .048), right at the conventional threshold — worth treating as a fragile finding at this stage rather than a confirmed one.

**District classification and Range school status both remain strong and significant**, essentially unchanged in direction from Model 2 (Dem_Desc even strengthens slightly), and average unemployment rate remains significant as well (OR ≈ 1.05 per unit, p = .003).

**English learner status remains non-significant throughout this entire sequence** (OR ≈ 0.77, p = .149), consistent with Models 1 and 2 — no relationship with regional completion at any stage.

**Overall Interpretation**

Adding high school accomplishments produces a very large improvement in model fit (likelihood ratio test: Δdeviance = 1,033.23, df = 7, p \< .001; AIC decreases from 16,687.1 to 15,667.9). **Took-ACT's effect here (OR ≈ 6.58) is the largest coefficient found anywhere in this project** — ACT engagement is an extraordinarily strong predictor of completing postsecondary education regionally rather than elsewhere. Special Education status and Asian/Pacific Islander status both lose significance once academic accomplishments are considered, while Black graduates newly emerge as significant — a genuine reshuffling of which demographic disparities are independent versus explained by academic engagement. Economic status, American Indian identity, district classification, and Range school status all remain significant, confirming real, independent relationships with where completers finish their credential.

Model fit: AIC = 15,667.9 (down from 16,687.1 in Model 2); Δdeviance = 1,033.23 on 7 df, p \< .001; n = 12,606 in both models.


## DV3 Summary: What Predicts Postsecondary Completion Within the Region (College Completers Only)

Across all three models, this analysis identifies district geography and ACT engagement as the two dominant forces shaping where postsecondary completers finish their credential, alongside several demographic patterns that shift meaningfully once academic accomplishments are considered.

**Took-ACT produces the largest single coefficient found anywhere in this project.** Students who took the ACT show more than six times the odds of completing their credential within the region compared to non-test-takers (OR ≈ 6.58, p \< .001). Among test-takers, the familiar crossover reappears: each additional composite point predicts lower odds of regional completion (OR ≈ 0.895 per point, p \< .001) — simply engaging with the ACT is strongly protective for staying regional, while strong performance specifically predicts completing elsewhere.

**District classification shows the largest geographic effects found anywhere in this project, and they strengthen rather than attenuate as other variables are added.** Graduates from Urban/town/rural mix districts show more than double the odds of regional completion relative to Entirely rural districts throughout the sequence (OR ≈ 2.36–2.52), and Town/rural mix districts show a similarly strong, stable effect (OR ≈ 1.93–2.06). Range school status adds a further, independent effect on top of district classification (OR ≈ 1.36–1.66 across models) — geography matters substantially more for *where* a completer finishes their credential than it does for workforce outcomes afterward.

**Special Education status loses significance entirely once academic accomplishments are considered — a real reversal, not a data artifact.** Significant and substantial in the demographics-only and characteristics models (OR ≈ 1.87–1.89), Special Ed status falls to non-significance in the final model (OR ≈ 1.19, p = .109) — its apparent tendency toward regional completion appears to run through academic engagement patterns rather than Special Ed status operating independently.

**Economic status remains significant throughout, though substantially attenuated.** OR weakens from ≈ 1.68 (Model 2) to ≈ 1.38 (Model 3) — academic engagement explains some, but far from all, of economically disadvantaged completers' tendency to complete regionally.

**Race/Ethnicity findings shift meaningfully across the sequence, with no single stable pattern.** American Indian graduates remain significant across all three models (OR ≈ 1.25–1.45), showing a consistent tendency toward regional completion. Asian/Pacific Islander graduates are significant in the demographics-only and characteristics models (OR ≈ 0.66) but lose significance once academic accomplishments are added (OR ≈ 0.94) — their apparent disadvantage runs through academic engagement rather than being independent of it. Black graduates show the opposite trajectory: non-significant in the first two models, then significant in the final model (OR ≈ 0.68, p = .035) — a disparity only detectable once academic accomplishments are fully accounted for. Hispanic graduates and English learner status remain non-significant throughout the entire sequence.

**SAT and AP exam participation both show a strong, stable negative relationship with regional completion**, consistent with their role throughout this project — both identify completers oriented toward postsecondary options outside the region (SAT: OR ≈ 0.39; AP: OR ≈ 0.72 in the final model).

**CTE Concentrator/Completer status shows an independent, positive relationship with regional completion, while CTE Participant status does not** — only the deeper level of CTE engagement holds up once other accomplishment variables are considered.

**PSEO participation shows no relationship with regional completion at any stage** — consistent with the pattern found in every other model sequence in this project.

**Local wages and unemployment rate both show a positive, strengthening relationship with regional completion.** Local wages grows to an extremely large effect in the final model (OR ≈ 7.95, though with a wide confidence interval reflecting real imprecision), and unemployment rate remains significant and stable (OR ≈ 1.05–1.07 per unit) — both consistent with the opportunity-cost pattern found for postsecondary completion overall, though here the relationship concerns *where* students complete rather than *whether* they do.

**Gender shows a weakening relationship across the sequence**, moving from clearly significant in Models 1–2 (OR ≈ 0.86–0.87) to only marginally significant in the final model (OR ≈ 0.92, p = .048) — worth treating as a fragile finding at the fully specified stage rather than a confirmed one.

<br>

# Prep DV4 Data

Another post-secondary independent variable that was strongly associated with workforce participation outcomes was the highest credential earned by an individual. This analysis will explore what characteristics are associated with earned credentials.

```{r}
model_vars_dv4<- c("Gender", "RaceEthnicity", "economic.status", "SpecialEdStatus",
                   "english.learner", "Dem_Desc", "range.school", "avg.wages.pct.state", "avg.unemp.rate",
                   "pseo.participant", "took.ACT", "ACTCompositeScore", "ap.exam", "sat.taken",
                   "cte.achievement","highest.cred.level")

master.model.dv4 <- master %>%
  filter(grad.year > 2010,
         grad.year <= 2019,
         ps.grad == "Y",
         highest.cred.level != "Did not graduate ps",
         RaceEthnicity != "Unknown") %>%
  select(PersonID, all_of(model_vars_dv4)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(pseo.participant)) %>%
  mutate(highest.cred.level = ifelse(highest.cred.level %in% c("Associate degree", "Less than Associate Degree"), "Associate or lesser credential", highest.cred.level),
         highest.cred.level = fct_relevel(highest.cred.level, "Bachelor degree or higher"),
         Gender = fct_relevel(Gender, "M"),
         RaceEthnicity = fct_relevel(RaceEthnicity, "White"),
         economic.status = as_factor(economic.status),
         economic.status = fct_relevel(economic.status, "0"),
         SpecialEdStatus = as.character(SpecialEdStatus),
         SpecialEdStatus = fct_relevel(SpecialEdStatus, "0"),
         english.learner = as_factor(english.learner),
         english.learner = fct_relevel(english.learner, "0"),
         Dem_Desc = fct_relevel(Dem_Desc, "Entirely rural"),
         range.school = fct_relevel(range.school, "Non-range school"),
         pseo.participant = as.character(pseo.participant),
         pseo.participant = fct_relevel(pseo.participant, "0"),
         took.ACT = fct_relevel(took.ACT, "No"),
         ACTCompositeScore.filled = ifelse(is.na(ACTCompositeScore), 0, ACTCompositeScore),
         sat.taken = as_factor(sat.taken),
         sat.taken = fct_relevel(sat.taken, "0"),
         ap.exam = as_factor(ap.exam),
         ap.exam = fct_relevel(ap.exam, "0"),
         cte.achievement = fct_relevel(cte.achievement, "No CTE"))

```

# Modeling: Credential Earned - college completers only

## Model 1: Demographics

This model estimates the association between demographic characteristics and earning an Associate degree or lesser credential (versus a Bachelor's degree or higher), restricted to postsecondary completers (n = 12,651). The outcome is coded 1 = Associate-or-lesser credential, 0 = Bachelor's degree or higher — so an odds ratio above 1 indicates *lower* educational attainment relative to Bachelor's, not a positive outcome in the sense used elsewhere in this project.

**Special Education status and economic disadvantage show by far the largest effects found anywhere in this project.**

- **Special Education status:** approximately 5.2 times higher odds of earning an Associate-or-lesser credential rather than a Bachelor's (OR ≈ 5.19, CI: 4.191–6.477) — the single largest coefficient found in any model across this entire analysis.
- **Economic disadvantage:** approximately 2.5 times higher odds of the same (OR ≈ 2.54).

Both results make substantive sense and are consistent with everything found in DV2: these two groups face substantial barriers to completing a four-year degree specifically, even though (per DV3) those who do complete tend to complete regionally.

**Gender shows a large, clean effect in the opposite direction from Special Ed/economic status.**

- **Female graduates:** approximately 36% lower odds of an Associate-or-lesser credential relative to male graduates (OR ≈ 0.64) — meaning female completers are considerably more likely to hold a Bachelor's degree or higher. This is directionally consistent with DV2, where female graduates showed substantially higher odds of completing college at all — the pattern extends here to completing at the *higher* credential level specifically.

**Race/Ethnicity shows a mixed and, in one case, quite large effect.**

- **Asian/Pacific Islander graduates:** approximately 68% lower odds of an Associate-or-lesser credential (OR ≈ 0.32) — meaning Asian/Pacific Islander completers are considerably more likely to hold a Bachelor's degree or higher, the largest Race/Ethnicity effect found in this model.
- **American Indian graduates:** approximately 44% higher odds of an Associate-or-lesser credential (OR ≈ 1.44) — the opposite direction from Asian/Pacific Islander graduates.
- **Black and Hispanic graduates:** not statistically significant, likely reflecting reduced power given small cell sizes in this completers-only population (n = 138 and n = 106, respectively).

**English learner status is significant, though with a wide confidence interval.** OR ≈ 1.72 (CI: 1.148–2.622) — English learner completers show higher odds of an Associate-or-lesser credential.

**Overall Interpretation**

At the demographics-only stage, Special Education status and economic disadvantage stand out as by far the strongest predictors of credential level examined anywhere in this project — both showing that these groups are considerably more likely to complete at the sub-baccalaureate level. This is directionally consistent with, and adds nuance to, the DV2 finding that these same groups face substantial barriers to completing college at all: among those who do complete, they are also considerably more likely to complete a shorter, more technical credential rather than a four-year degree. Gender and Race/Ethnicity (particularly Asian/Pacific Islander) show meaningful effects as well, with women and Asian/Pacific Islander completers more likely to hold a Bachelor's degree.

**Model fit:** AIC = 15,898.8; n = 12,651.

```{r}

)
```

## Model 2: Demographics + High School Characteristics

This model adds district rural/urban classification, Range school status, local average wages, and local average unemployment rate to the demographic baseline, restricted to postsecondary completers (n = 12,651). Recall the outcome here is coded 1 = Associate degree or less, 0 = Bachelor's degree or higher, so positive coefficients indicate higher odds of a sub-baccalaureate credential.

**Range school status shows a strong, independent relationship with sub-baccalaureate attainment.** Range graduates show 57% higher odds of completing an Associate degree or less rather than a Bachelor's degree (OR ≈ 1.57, p \< .001) — consistent with Range communities' documented orientation toward technical and associate-level credentials tied to regional industry.

**Local wages shows a striking reversal from every other DV in this project.** Higher local wages relative to the state average predict substantially *lower* odds of sub-baccalaureate attainment (OR ≈ 0.29, p = .003) — in other words, higher local wages predict *higher* odds of Bachelor's-level completion. This is the opposite direction from what higher wages predicted for overall postsecondary completion (DV2, where higher wages discouraged completion) and for completing within the region (DV3, where higher wages encouraged regional completion) — a genuinely distinct relationship for this specific outcome, worth stating plainly rather than trying to force it into the same "opportunity cost" framing used elsewhere.

**District classification shows no significant relationship here** — a sharp contrast with DV3, where Dem_Desc produced some of the largest effects in this project. Town/rural mix is clearly non-significant (OR ≈ 1.01, p = .932), and Urban/town/rural mix only approaches significance without crossing it (OR ≈ 0.85, p = .088). Credential *level* appears to have little to do with district geography, even though credential *location* (DV3) was strongly tied to it.

**All demographic effects from Model 1 remain essentially unchanged.** Gender (OR ≈ 0.65), economic status (OR ≈ 2.48), Special Education status (OR ≈ 5.31), English learner status (OR ≈ 1.73), American Indian graduates (OR ≈ 1.44), and Asian/Pacific Islander graduates (OR ≈ 0.34) all hold steady in direction and magnitude from Model 1. Special Education status in particular remains an extraordinarily large effect — Special Ed completers show more than five times the odds of a sub-baccalaureate credential relative to a Bachelor's degree.

**Average unemployment rate remains non-significant** (OR ≈ 1.00, p = .934).

**Overall Interpretation**

Adding high school characteristics significantly improves model fit (likelihood ratio test: Δdeviance = 93.58, df = 5, p \< .001; AIC decreases from 15,898.8 to 15,815.2). **Range school status and local wages are the standout findings in this block, and the wage direction is genuinely distinct from every other DV in this project** — here, higher local wages push toward Bachelor's-level attainment rather than away from postsecondary engagement generally or toward regional completion specifically. District classification, by contrast, shows essentially no relationship with credential level, despite being one of the strongest predictors of completion location in DV3 — a useful reminder that "where" and "what level" are separate questions with different drivers. All five demographic effects from Model 1 remain fully intact.

Model fit: AIC = 15,815.2 (down from 15,898.8 in Model 1); Δdeviance = 93.58 on 5 df, p \< .001; n = 12,651 in both models.

```{r}
model2_dv4 <- glm(
  highest.cred.level ~
    Gender +
    RaceEthnicity +
    economic.status +
    SpecialEdStatus +
    english.learner +
    Dem_Desc +
    range.school +
    avg.wages.pct.state +
    avg.unemp.rate,
  family = binomial,
  data = master.model.dv4
)

summary(model2_dv4)

nobs(model1_dv4)
nobs(model2_dv4)

AIC(model1_dv4)
AIC(model2_dv4)

exp(cbind(OR = coef(model2_dv4), confint(model2_dv4)))

anova(model1_dv4, model2_dv4, test = "Chisq")


or_plot <- tidy(model2_dv4, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(
    # Make labels nicer (edit these replacements to match your exact factor labels)
    term = str_replace_all(term, c(
      "RaceEthnicity" = "Race: ",
      "economic.status" = "Economic status: ",
      "SpecialEdStatus" = "Special Ed: ",
      "pseo.participant" = "PSEO: ",
      "cte.achievement" = "CTE: ",
      "MCA.M" = "MCA Math",
      "highest.cred.level" = "Highest credential"
    )),
    # Put most important effects near the top (optional: tweak ordering later)
    term = fct_reorder(term, estimate)
  )


ggplot(or_plot, aes(x = estimate, y = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.5, 0.75, 1.25, 1.5, 2),
             color = "grey85") +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
    orientation = "y",
    width = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2),
    labels = c("0.5", "0.75", "1.0", "1.25", "1.5", "2.0")
  ) +
  theme_line +
  labs(
    x = "Odds ratio (log scale)",
    y = NULL
  )
```

## Model 3: Demographics + High School Characteristics + High School Accomplishments

This model adds PSEO participation, ACT participation and score, SAT participation, AP exam participation, and CTE achievement to the growing specification, restricted to postsecondary completers (n = 12,651). Recall the outcome is coded 1 = Associate degree or less, 0 = Bachelor's degree or higher.

**ACT shows the same crossover pattern found throughout this project, at the largest scale seen anywhere in this entire analysis.** Taking the ACT shows an enormous positive association with earning an Associate-or-lesser credential (OR ≈ 14.12, p \< .001) — students who took the ACT are far more likely to complete at the sub-baccalaureate level than those who never tested. Among test-takers, each additional composite point predicts the opposite direction (OR ≈ 0.816 per point, p \< .001): higher scores predict a Bachelor's degree instead. Read together: ACT engagement without strong performance still predicts a shorter, more technical credential pathway.

**Black graduates become significant here for the first time in this sequence — a genuinely new finding, not present in Models 1 or 2.** OR ≈ 0.55 (CI: 0.368-0.811, p = .003) — once academic accomplishments are accounted for, Black completers show meaningfully higher odds of earning a Bachelor's degree specifically.

**English learner status remains non-significant here — and this is a genuine, standalone null, not an artifact of any missingness control, since none is anywhere in this specification.** OR ≈ 0.84 (CI: 0.549-1.319, p = .448). Credential level shows no independent relationship with English learner status at any stage of this model sequence.

**PSEO participation shows a clear, significant effect specific to this outcome.** OR ≈ 0.66 (p \< .001) — PSEO participants are notably more likely to complete a Bachelor's degree rather than an Associate-or-lesser credential. This is a different role for PSEO than seen in the other DVs in this project: elsewhere it predicted completion generally or showed no independent effect, while here it specifically predicts higher credential attainment among those who do complete.

**CTE achievement shows its strongest positive effect anywhere in this project.** CTE Concentrator/Completer status: OR ≈ 1.61 (p \< .001) — the largest CTE coefficient found in any model sequence. CTE Participant: OR ≈ 1.14 (p = .010). This makes strong substantive sense — CTE pathways are more likely to lead directly into Associate-level and technical credentials by design.

**AP exam and SAT participation both point toward Bachelor's attainment**, consistent with their role throughout this project (AP: OR ≈ 0.74, p \< .001; SAT: OR ≈ 0.61, p = .007).

**Average local unemployment rate becomes significant and meaningfully sized for the first time in this sequence** (OR ≈ 0.89 per unit, p \< .001) — higher local unemployment predicts lower odds of an Associate-or-lesser credential (i.e., predicts Bachelor's attainment instead). This is a counterintuitive direction worth flagging plainly rather than forcing into a tidy explanation, consistent with this project's general practice of not over-narrating a modest, less-intuitive coefficient.

**Local wages loses the significance it showed in Model 2.** OR ≈ 0.56 (CI: 0.216-1.460, p = .237) — its apparent relationship with credential level appears to run through academic engagement rather than operating independently.

**Demographic effects persist but attenuate substantially.** Gender (OR ≈ 0.73), economic status (OR ≈ 1.90, down from ≈ 2.48), and Special Ed status (OR ≈ 2.16, down sharply from ≈ 5.31) all remain significant but meaningfully weaker — academic engagement explains a substantial share of these disparities, though far from all of it. Asian/Pacific Islander graduates remain significant and large (OR ≈ 0.39, p \< .001). American Indian graduates lose significance (OR ≈ 1.09, p = .448), a real change from Models 1-2.

**District classification and Range school status both weaken.** Dem_Desc remains non-significant, as in Model 2. Range school status, significant and substantial in Model 2 (OR ≈ 1.57), weakens to only marginal significance here (OR ≈ 1.13, p = .031) — its apparent relationship with credential level runs substantially through academic accomplishments.

**Overall Interpretation**

Adding high school accomplishments produces by far the largest improvement in model fit found anywhere in this project (likelihood ratio test: Δdeviance = 3,060.72, df = 7, p \< .001; AIC decreases sharply from 15,815.2 to 12,768.5). **Academic achievement and college-preparatory engagement are overwhelmingly the dominant forces shaping credential level — far more so than demographics or geography.** The ACT crossover, at the largest scale found anywhere in this project, and CTE's strong positive association with Associate-level attainment are the standout findings. Black graduates emerge as a newly significant, independent predictor once academic engagement is considered, while American Indian graduates and Range school status both lose the significance they showed in earlier models. English learner status remains a clean, consistent null throughout this entire sequence.

Model fit: AIC = 12,768.5 (down from 15,815.2 in Model 2); Δdeviance = 3,060.72 on 7 df, p \< .001; n = 12,651 in both models.

```{r}
model3_dv4 <- glm(
  highest.cred.level ~
    Gender +
    RaceEthnicity +
    economic.status +
    SpecialEdStatus +
    english.learner +
    Dem_Desc +
    range.school +
    avg.wages.pct.state +
    avg.unemp.rate +
    pseo.participant +
    took.ACT +
    ACTCompositeScore.filled +
    ap.exam + 
    sat.taken +
    cte.achievement,
    family = binomial,
  data = master.model.dv4
)

summary(model3_dv4)

nobs(model1_dv4)
nobs(model2_dv4)
nobs(model3_dv4)

AIC(model1_dv4)
AIC(model2_dv4)
AIC(model3_dv4)

exp(cbind(OR = coef(model3_dv4), confint(model3_dv4)))

anova(model1_dv4, model2_dv4, model3_dv4, test = "Chisq")


or_plot <- tidy(model3_dv4, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(
    # Make labels nicer (edit these replacements to match your exact factor labels)
    term = str_replace_all(term, c(
      "RaceEthnicity" = "Race: ",
      "economic.status" = "Economic status: ",
      "SpecialEdStatus" = "Special Ed: ",
      "pseo.participant" = "PSEO: ",
      "cte.achievement" = "CTE: ",
      "MCA.M" = "MCA Math",
      "highest.cred.level" = "Highest credential"
    )),
    # Put most important effects near the top (optional: tweak ordering later)
    term = fct_reorder(term, estimate)
  )


ggplot(or_plot, aes(x = estimate, y = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.5, 0.75, 1.25, 1.5, 2),
             color = "grey85") +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
    orientation = "y",
    width = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2),
    labels = c("0.5", "0.75", "1.0", "1.25", "1.5", "2.0")
  ) +
  theme_line +

    x = "Odds ratio (log scale)",
    y = NULL
```

## DV4 Summary: What Predicts Sub-Baccalaureate Credential Attainment (College Completers Only)

Across all three models, academic accomplishments emerge as overwhelmingly the dominant force shaping whether a postsecondary completer earns a Bachelor's degree or an Associate-or-lesser credential — far more so than demographics or geography, a genuinely different pattern than found in any other DV in this project. Recall the outcome is coded 1 = Associate degree or less, 0 = Bachelor's degree or higher, so all odds ratios below describe the odds of the sub-baccalaureate outcome unless noted otherwise.

**ACT engagement produces the single largest coefficient found anywhere in this entire analysis, and shows the clearest crossover pattern of any DV.** Simply taking the ACT is associated with dramatically higher odds of completing at the sub-baccalaureate level (OR ≈ 14.12) — an enormous effect, even relative to the large ACT effects found elsewhere in this project. Among test-takers, the direction reverses: each additional composite point predicts substantially lower odds of a sub-baccalaureate credential (OR ≈ 0.816 per point) — higher scorers complete Bachelor's degrees instead. Read together: ACT engagement without strong performance predicts a shorter, more technical credential pathway, while strong performance predicts the opposite.

**Special Education status shows the single largest demographic effect found anywhere in this project, though it attenuates substantially once academic accomplishments are considered.** Special Ed completers show over five times the odds of a sub-baccalaureate credential in the demographics-only and characteristics models (OR ≈ 5.19–5.31), weakening to just over double the odds once academic engagement is accounted for (OR ≈ 2.16) — a real, substantial reduction, but the effect remains large and clearly significant throughout.

**Economic status shows a similarly large, stable pattern.** Economically disadvantaged completers show substantially higher odds of a sub- baccalaureate credential across all three models (OR ≈ 1.90–2.54), weakening somewhat once academic accomplishments enter the model but remaining one of the strongest and most consistent predictors in this sequence.

**English learner status is significant early in the sequence but resolves to a clean, genuine null once academic accomplishments are considered — with no missingness control anywhere in the specification.** Significant in the demographics-only and characteristics models (OR ≈ 1.72–1.73, predicting higher odds of a sub-baccalaureate credential), English learner status loses significance entirely in the final model (OR ≈ 0.84). Whatever drives this early relationship appears to run through academic engagement rather than English learner status operating independently.

**Race/Ethnicity findings shift meaningfully across the sequence.** Asian/Pacific Islander graduates show a large, stable, significant relationship with Bachelor's-level attainment throughout all three models (OR ≈ 0.32–0.39) — the most consistent Race/Ethnicity finding in this sequence. American Indian graduates are significant in the demographics- only and characteristics models (OR ≈ 1.44) but lose significance once academic accomplishments are added (OR ≈ 1.09). Black graduates show the opposite trajectory: non-significant in the first two models, then significant in the final model (OR ≈ 0.55) — a disparity favoring Bachelor's attainment that only emerges once academic engagement is fully accounted for. Hispanic graduates remain non-significant throughout.

**PSEO participation shows a distinct role for this outcome compared to every other DV in this project.** OR ≈ 0.66 — PSEO participants are notably more likely to complete a Bachelor's degree specifically, a different relationship than PSEO showed for completion generally or for regional attachment, where it predicted little or showed a different direction entirely.

**CTE achievement shows its strongest positive effect anywhere in this project.** CTE Concentrator/Completer status (OR ≈ 1.61) is the largest CTE coefficient found in any model sequence, with CTE Participant status showing a smaller but still significant effect (OR ≈ 1.14) — both substantively sensible, since CTE pathways are designed to lead directly into Associate-level and technical credentials.

**AP exam and SAT participation both predict Bachelor's-level attainment**, consistent with their role throughout this project (AP: OR ≈ 0.74; SAT: OR ≈ 0.61).

**Gender shows a large, stable, significant relationship throughout**, with female completers consistently more likely to earn a Bachelor's degree (OR ≈ 0.65–0.73 across all three models).

**District classification shows no relationship with credential level at any stage** — a sharp contrast with this project's findings on completion *location*, where geography was one of the strongest predictors. Range school status is significant in the characteristics model (OR ≈ 1.57) but weakens to only marginal significance once academic accomplishments are considered (OR ≈ 1.13).

**Local wages and unemployment rate both show effects that emerge or fade unpredictably across the sequence, worth treating as modest and provisional rather than forcing into a single coherent story.** Local wages is significant and protective toward Bachelor's attainment in the characteristics model (OR ≈ 0.29) but loses significance once academic accomplishments are added (OR ≈ 0.56). Local unemployment rate is non- significant until the final model, where it becomes significant in a counterintuitive direction (OR ≈ 0.89 per unit — higher unemployment predicting Bachelor's attainment rather than the reverse) — worth noting plainly rather than over-explaining.

<br>

# Executive Summary

This analysis used logistic regression to confirm and refine patterns identified in earlier descriptive work on post-high school pathways for Northeast Minnesota graduates. Five models were built, each isolating a different piece of the pathway: whether graduates stay in the region long term, whether they complete college, where they complete it, and what type of credential they earn.

Four consistent themes emerged across all five models:

1.  **Geography does different jobs at different stages.** High school district type, Range school status, and local economic conditions strongly predict whether a graduate stays in the region for work and where they complete their postsecondary education — but have almost no bearing on whether they complete college at all, or what type of credential they earn once they do. Geography shapes *where* things happen, not *whether* or *what*.

2.  **CTE and ACT represent two distinct, opposing pathways, and this project's clearest, largest, and most consistent finding.** Career and technical education consistently predicts staying in the region and completing shorter, more technical credentials. ACT engagement shows a striking split, visible in every model: simply taking the test predicts staying regional and completing an Associate-level credential — in one model, taking the ACT alone predicts fourteen times higher odds of a sub-baccalaureate credential — while scoring well on it predicts leaving the region and completing a Bachelor's degree instead. These aren't two versions of the same "college-readiness" signal; they represent different, sometimes opposing, routes through the pipeline.

3.  **English learner status tells two entirely different stories, depending on which outcome is examined — one of the most important findings in this analysis.** For the full graduating population, English learner status is a robust, independent predictor of reduced odds of sustained regional workforce attachment, holding up fully alongside demographics, geography, academic accomplishments, and postsecondary completion — this is a real, standalone disparity, not explained by anything else in the model. But among students who go on to complete a postsecondary credential, English learner status shows no relationship at all with regional attachment, completion location, or credential level. In other words: the English learner disparity in this data is entirely about workforce attachment for those who don't complete a credential — it is not a story about academic preparation, and it disappears entirely once a student completes college.

4.  **Demographic disparities are real, but some are explained by how students engage with school, while others are not.** Economic disadvantage and Special Education status both show very large effects early in the postsecondary-completion and credential-level models, and both weaken substantially — though remain significant — once academic engagement is added, indicating that some, not all, of the disparity operates through unequal access to or engagement with CTE, PSEO, and testing pathways. Black, Hispanic, and Asian/Pacific Islander graduates tell a different story: their disparities in regional workforce attachment and postsecondary completion largely persist regardless of academic engagement, and in several models a disparity only becomes visible once academic engagement is fully accounted for — these are not explained away by anything measured in this analysis.

The single largest and most consistent finding across every model, and the one most directly relevant to the project's regional workforce mission, is that **geography — where a student completes their postsecondary education — matters more than what credential they earn.** Graduating within the region was the strongest predictor of sustained regional employment found among completers. But credential type is not irrelevant either: among college completers specifically, Associate-level and technical credentials showed a real, independent, additional association with staying regional, on top of the location effect.

<br>

# The Story This Data Tells

Picture a graduating class in Northeast Minnesota. What happens to them over the next five, ten years, and why?

**The pipeline starts to split immediately, along economic and ability- status lines.** Economically disadvantaged students and students with disabilities are considerably less likely to complete any postsecondary credential at all — among the strongest demographic patterns in the entire analysis. But these same students, if they do complete a credential, don't carry that disadvantage forward in the same form: much of what predicted non-completion in the first place turns out to run through *how* these students engaged with high school academically — CTE involvement, ACT participation, PSEO — rather than being a fixed consequence of the demographic category itself.

**English learners face a genuinely different, more specific barrier — one that shows up at the front door, not throughout the building.** English learners are meaningfully less likely to be sustainably attached to the regional workforce, and this disadvantage holds up fully no matter what else is accounted for — academic preparation, geography, whether they attempted college at all. But this barrier is entirely specific to students who don't go on to complete a postsecondary credential. Among English learners who do complete a credential, there is no detectable disadvantage in staying regional, completing locally, or the level of credential earned. The English learner story in this data is a workforce- attachment story, not an academic-preparation story — and it resolves itself completely once a credential is in hand.

**For those who do complete college, a second split happens — not about whether they succeed, but about where and how.** Two students with identical demographics can take very different paths depending on how they engaged with high school. A student who took CTE courses and engaged with the ACT — regardless of score — is likely on a track toward a shorter, technical credential completed close to home, and likely to stay in the regional workforce afterward. A student who scored well on the ACT and pursued AP coursework or the SAT is likely headed toward a four-year degree, often completed outside the region — and less likely to return.

**This is the pipeline's central tension, visible in every model in this analysis: the very things that predict finishing a four-year degree — strong test scores, AP coursework, SAT participation — are the same things that predict leaving the region.** Meanwhile, the pathways this project's organization has less institutional visibility into promoting — CTE, technical credentials, PSEO — are consistently the ones associated with staying.

**Geography reinforces this tension rather than resolving it.** Students from more urban districts and Range school communities are considerably more likely to complete their postsecondary education within the region — this is the single largest set of effects found anywhere in this analysis — but this same geographic advantage barely registers when predicting whether a student completes college at all, or what type of credential they earn. Geography shapes *where* the funnel empties out, not how big the funnel is or what flows through it.

**And underneath all of this, demographic disparities persist — but not always for the same reasons, and not always visible at the same point in the analysis.** Some disparities — Special Education status, economic disadvantage, and, among completers, American Indian identity and Range school status — shrink substantially once a student's academic engagement is accounted for, suggesting these groups may be channeled toward or away from certain pathways based on how school systems engage them, not fixed traits tied to the demographic category itself. Other disparities — particularly for Black, Hispanic, and Asian/Pacific Islander graduates — persist even after accounting for every other factor in this analysis, and in several cases only become visible once academic engagement is fully accounted for, suggesting they are not artifacts of differential program access but something this analysis cannot fully explain.

**Put together, the data describes a region whose workforce retention depends less on whether people leave for stronger opportunities elsewhere and more on which door they walked through in high school** — CTE and modest ACT engagement lead back to the region; AP coursework, strong ACT scores, and SAT participation lead away from it. This is not a story about talent leaving because the region has nothing to offer skilled workers — it's a story about two genuinely different pipelines, one regionally anchored and one not, both running through the same high schools at the same time.
